definitions.definition: A study that tries to connect physics, consciousness, and God using math and logic.
definitions.example: Like a science that studies how spiritual truths might work like physical laws.

definitions.definition: When different pieces of evidence from different fields all point to the same conclusion.
definitions.example: Like if your teacher, your friend, and your mom all separately told you the same answer to a question.

definitions.definition: Relating to God or a god; something holy or sacred.
definitions.example: People might say a beautiful sunset is a divine creation.

definitions.definition: The smallest piece of a chemical element, made of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
definitions.example: Everything around you, like your desk or your phone, is made of atoms.

definitions.definition: The tiny, dense center of an atom, containing protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: If an atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea in the middle.

definitions.definition: The study of numbers, shapes, patterns, and the relationships between them.
definitions.example: Adding, subtracting, geometry, and algebra are all parts of mathematics.

definitions.definition: The surprising fact that math, which humans invented in their minds, perfectly describes how the real universe works.
definitions.example: It's like if you made up a game with rules, and then found out those rules actually control how your car engine runs.

definitions.definition: The smallest possible amount of something, like energy; also describes the weird rules that tiny particles follow.
definitions.example: At the quantum level, particles can be in two places at once, which is impossible for big things like baseballs.

definitions.definition: Relating to the whole universe, especially the vast space between stars and galaxies.
definitions.example: A cosmic event would be something like a star exploding or a galaxy colliding with another.

definitions.definition: The branch of philosophy that asks what is real, what exists, and why anything exists at all.
definitions.example: Asking 'Is time real?' or 'Do numbers exist?' are metaphysical questions.

definitions.definition: Basic beliefs or assumptions that you accept as true before you can start reasoning about something.
definitions.example: Before you can do a science experiment, you have to assume that your eyes and tools are telling you the truth.

definitions.definition: True for everyone, not just based on personal feelings or opinions.
definitions.example: The fact that water freezes at 0°C is objective; whether you like cold weather is subjective.

definitions.definition: The mental abilities your brain uses to think, learn, remember, and understand things.
definitions.example: Your memory, your ability to pay attention, and your logic skills are all cognitive faculties.

definitions.definition: The assumption that the laws of nature are the same everywhere in the universe and at all times.
definitions.example: We assume that gravity works the same way on Mars tomorrow as it does on Earth today.

definitions.definition: Believing in a personal God or gods who created and interacts with the world.
definitions.example: Christianity, Islam, and Judaism are theistic religions.

definitions.definition: Believing that only nature and physical matter exist, and that there is no God or spiritual world.
definitions.example: A naturalistic view says that everything, including your thoughts, is just the result of physical processes in your brain.

definitions.definition: A problem in philosophy showing that any attempt to prove something is true leads to an endless chain, a circle, or a starting point you just have to accept.
definitions.example: It's like trying to prove a dictionary is correct: you look up a word, but that definition uses other words, and those need defining, and it never ends.

definitions.definition: An endless chain of causes or reasons, where each step depends on a previous step that never stops.
definitions.example: If you say 'I know it because my teacher said so,' and then ask 'how does your teacher know?' and keep asking, you get an infinite regress.

definitions.definition: A type of reasoning where the conclusion is also used as one of the premises, so it goes in a circle.
definitions.example: Saying 'The Bible is true because it is the word of God, and we know it's the word of God because the Bible says so' is a circular argument.

definitions.definition: A starting rule or assumption that is chosen without a deeper reason, just accepted as true to build on.
definitions.example: In geometry, one axiom is that a straight line can be drawn between any two points. We just accept it without proof.

definitions.definition: Basic statements or rules that are assumed to be true without proof, used as a starting point for other reasoning.
definitions.example: In math, 'if a=b and b=c, then a=c' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: The quality of being understandable or making sense to the human mind.
definitions.example: The fact that we can figure out how stars work shows the universe has intelligibility.

definitions.definition: Relating to the study of God and religious beliefs.
definitions.example: A theological question might be 'Does God have a plan for everyone?'

definitions.definition: The logical step of concluding that something was made by an intelligent mind because it is too complex and specific to have happened by chance.
definitions.example: If you find a watch on a beach, you infer it was designed, not that the ocean waves made it by accident.

definitions.definition: A pattern that is both complicated and matches a specific meaning, which is a sign of being designed by a mind.
definitions.example: A sentence in a book has complex specified information; random letters do not.

definitions.definition: The observation that the universe's physical laws and constants are set to very precise values that allow life to exist, as if they were adjusted on purpose.
definitions.example: If gravity were even slightly stronger, the universe would have collapsed right after the Big Bang, so it seems 'fine-tuned' for us.

definitions.definition: The set of rules by which information in DNA is translated into proteins, the building blocks of life.
definitions.example: The genetic code is like a language with four letters (A, T, C, G) that spells out instructions for your body.

definitions.definition: A property of a pattern that is both very unlikely to occur by chance and matches a specific, meaningful arrangement.
definitions.example: A string of letters that spells 'HELLO' has specified complexity; a random string like 'XJQZ' does not.

definitions.definition: When complex patterns or behaviors arise from the interactions of many simpler parts, without a central planner.
definitions.example: A flock of birds moving together is an emergent behavior; no single bird is directing the whole flock.

definitions.definition: When a system naturally forms an ordered pattern without any outside control or design.
definitions.example: Snowflakes forming their beautiful, symmetrical shapes is an example of self-organization.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical collection of many separate universes, including our own, each possibly with different physical laws.
definitions.example: The multiverse idea is like saying our universe is just one bubble in a giant bubble bath of many universes.

definitions.definition: The central, most important part of an argument or structure that holds everything else together.
definitions.example: In an arch, the keystone is the top stone that locks all the other stones in place.

definitions.definition: A condition that must be met before something else can happen or be true.
definitions.example: Having a ticket is a precondition for entering a movie theater.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two structures that shows they have the same form or pattern, even if the things inside them are different.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines: the connections are the same, even though the map is on paper.

definitions.definition: The limits or rules that define the edges of a system and affect how it behaves.
definitions.example: For a game of soccer, the boundary conditions are the size of the field and the rules of the game.

definitions.definition: The ability for an experiment or result to be repeated by other people and get the same outcome.
definitions.example: If a scientist says a drug works, other scientists must be able to reproduce the result in their own labs.

definitions.definition: Good qualities like love, joy, peace, and patience that the Bible says come from having a relationship with God.
definitions.example: Someone who is very patient and kind even when things go wrong might be showing the fruit of the Spirit.

definitions.definition: A similarity in the way two different things are organized or built, even if the things themselves are different.
definitions.example: The organization of a company's departments can have a structural parallel to the branches of a tree.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how order and goodness (coherence) in a system change over time, depending on grace and decay.
definitions.example: It's like a formula that predicts whether a team will become more united or fall apart.

definitions.definition: A mathematical equation that describes how a quantity changes over time or space.
definitions.example: A differential equation can predict how fast a cup of coffee cools down, based on the temperature difference.

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that deals with heat, energy, and how they move and change.
definitions.example: Thermodynamics explains why ice melts in a warm room and why engines get hot.

definitions.definition: The study of how populations of living things change in size and composition over time.
definitions.example: Population dynamics can model how many rabbits and foxes there will be in a forest next year.

definitions.definition: The mathematical study of how information is measured, stored, and communicated.
definitions.example: Information theory is used to compress files on your computer and to make WiFi work.

definitions.definition: A measure of how ordered, unified, and 'good' a system is, on a scale from 0 to 1.
definitions.example: A well-organized team with a clear goal has high coherence; a chaotic, arguing team has low coherence.

definitions.definition: Something that brings order, structure, or goodness into a system, like grace, a good law, or a clear plan.
definitions.example: A good teacher who sets clear rules and helps students is an ordering force in a classroom.

definitions.definition: A mathematical rule that describes how something new is produced from existing potential.
definitions.example: A recipe is like a generative function: it takes ingredients (potential) and produces a cake.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the tendency for things to become more messy over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom naturally gets messier over time (entropy increases) unless you put in effort to clean it.

definitions.definition: The speed at which something breaks down, falls apart, or becomes less ordered.
definitions.example: The decay rate of a radioactive element tells you how fast it turns into other elements.

definitions.definition: Increasing or decreasing at a very fast rate, where the change is proportional to the current amount.
definitions.example: A virus spreading exponentially means each infected person infects several more, and the total cases skyrocket.

definitions.definition: A law of physics stating that the total disorder (entropy) of an isolated system always increases over time.
definitions.example: The Second Law is why you can't un-break an egg: the egg's molecules become more disordered.

definitions.definition: A computer program that helps mathematicians check their proofs for errors, like a super-precise spell-checker for logic.
definitions.example: If you write a math proof, Lean 4 can check every step to make sure you didn't make a mistake.

definitions.definition: A computer program that helps a person write and check a logical proof, ensuring every step is valid.
definitions.example: It's like a calculator for logic: you type in your reasoning, and the program checks if it's correct.

definitions.definition: The idea that the most basic, foundational layer of reality comes before and supports everything built on top of it.
definitions.example: In a house, the foundation has substrate priority over the walls and roof.

definitions.definition: A central mathematical formula in Theophysics that describes how coherence changes, combining many factors.
definitions.example: It's like the main equation that governs the whole system, similar to E=mc² for relativity.

definitions.definition: A mathematical fix in the Coherence Equation that prevents disorder from growing without limit, by adding a 'repair' factor.
definitions.example: It's like a self-correcting mechanism that stops things from falling apart completely.

definitions.definition: A property of the Master Equation where if any one factor becomes zero, the whole result becomes zero, like a chain breaking at its weakest link.
definitions.example: If you are making a cake and you forget the flour (one factor = 0), the whole cake collapses.

definitions.definition: A theoretical field in Theophysics, different from coherence, that represents a kind of potential or underlying structure.
definitions.example: Think of it like a background energy field that is always positive, unlike coherence which can be zero.

definitions.definition: A mathematical function in the Coherence Equation that represents how grace (unearned help or a new path) increases coherence without destroying it.
definitions.example: It's like a function that takes a messy room (low coherence) and makes it tidier without breaking anything.

definitions.definition: A proposed connection between a famous physics theorem (Noether's) and the Ten Commandments, suggesting both are about preserving what is good.
definitions.example: Noether's theorem says that for every symmetry in nature, there is a conserved quantity; the idea is that commandments conserve moral order.

definitions.definition: Tests that check whether two different systems have the same underlying structure (isomorphism), used to see if a model is valid.
definitions.example: It's like checking if a map of a subway is a good match for the actual subway lines.

definitions.definition: A new, positive way of living or behaving that is offered freely, instead of just punishing the old bad behavior.
definitions.example: Instead of just fining people for littering, a grace pathway would be to provide free trash bags and teach them why it's important.

definitions.definition: The belief that life has no meaning, purpose, or value.
definitions.example: Someone who feels that nothing matters and there is no point to anything might be described as a nihilist.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle'; in Christianity, it refers to Jesus Christ as the rational order behind the universe.
definitions.example: The Logos is like the 'operating system' of the universe that makes it logical and understandable.

definitions.definition: A pattern in real-world data that is the telltale sign of a specific cause or process.
definitions.example: A fingerprint at a crime scene is an empirical signature of a person being there.

definitions.definition: A way of calculating how likely something is, based on new evidence and your prior beliefs.
definitions.example: If you see dark clouds (evidence), Bayesian probability updates your belief that it will rain.

definitions.definition: A type of reasoning where you choose the explanation that makes the most sense out of all the possible ones.
